Everything an organism does is taken from an energy budget balanced between survival and reproductive capability. You can't claim leaving the nutrients intact as a new concept as it's something that's always been present in insecticide producing GMOs. The related problems lie in exactly what the energy costs are and therefore how much energy is lost that would otherwise be put into producing whatever crop is in question.

Part of the problem stems from our practice of agriculture in the first place. We have systematically bred plants to have favourable traits such as increased yield, faster growth, etc while removing defenses that come across as distasteful such as plant metabolites in the form of glucosinolates [like sinigrin in brassicae plants (gives the characteristic mustardy smell/taste) which is a notable reason why younger children often don't like such plants as their pre-pubescent body literally can't handle toxin levels as adults can]. The Solanaceae family of plants consists of tomatoes, tobacco plants, potatoes, eggplants, peppers/chillis as well as horticultural plants such as petunias. While modern tomatoes/potatoes/eggplants are edible with little concern to anyone there are still wild varieties that are deadly if consumed, hence the generic nickname the family sometimes gets of "deadly nightshades".
